48-040.r: Fort William College, Calcutta → founded 10 July 1800 by Lord Wellesley to train British civil servants in Indian languages (Persian, Hindustani).
48-040.t: Don't confuse the year: 1800, not 1802; purpose was training civil servants, not historical research.

48-042.r: Madan Mohan Malviya → vigorously advocated religious education in Indian universities; founded Banaras Hindu University (BHU), Varanasi, 1916; its Vice-Chancellor 1919-1939.

48-043.r: Annie Besant → founded Central Hindu School/College, Banaras (7 July 1898); it became the core of Banaras Hindu University (1916, with Malviya's efforts).
48-043.t: Don't confuse Annie Besant (Central Hindu College) with Malviya (founder of BHU itself).

48-045.r: Lord Hardinge (II), the Viceroy → laid foundation stone of Banaras Hindu University on 4 February 1916 (Basant Panchami).
48-045.t: Founder of BHU = Madan Mohan Malviya; foundation stone = Viceroy Lord Hardinge.

48-046.r: Banaras Hindu University, Varanasi (founded by Madan Mohan Malviya, 1916) → first to be declared a Central University among the options.

49-001.r: Printing press in India → introduced by the Portuguese at Goa in 1556 (first in Asia).

49-002.r: Bengal Gazette → first newspaper in India; English, Calcutta, started 1780 by James Augustus Hicky.

49-004.r: Lord Wellesley → first imposed press censorship (Censorship of the Press Act, 1799); Lord Hastings removed the strict censorship in 1818.

49-005.r: Vernacular Press Act 1878 → passed by Lord Lytton (1876-1880); repealed by Lord Ripon. Magistrates could demand bonds/security from Indian-language publishers.
49-005.h: L-L: Lytton Locked the vernacular press; R-R: Ripon Repealed.
hi: Vernacular Press Act (देशी भाषा समाचार पत्र अधिनियम)

49-010.r: Press freedom → bill began under William Bentinck, but the Press Act was passed in August 1835 by acting Governor-General Charles Metcalfe, 'Liberator of Indian Press'.
49-010.t: Don't credit Bentinck: the 1835 Press Act came under Metcalfe.

49-011.r: Surendra Nath Banerjee → first Indian jailed for his duty as a journalist (2 April 1883, for an article in 'The Bengalee').

49-012.r: Tarak Nath Das → started the newspaper 'Free Hindustan' in America.

49-013.r: Raja Ram Mohan Roy → Bengali weekly 'Sambad Kaumudi' (1821) and Persian weekly 'Mirat-ul-Akhbar' (1822).
49-013.t: Acting Governor-General John Adams banned unlicensed Indian press in 1823.

49-014.r: 'Indian Mirror' → daily from Calcutta; founded 1861 by Debendra Nath Tagore and Manmohan Ghosh; Keshav Chandra Sen in its editorial team.

49-015.r: Journal 'Ghadar' → first issue in Urdu on 1 November 1913; Gurmukhi edition from 9 December 1913; later also Marathi, Hindi, English, Gujarati, Pashto.

49-016.r: 'Ghadar' of the Ghadar Party (San Francisco, 1913; Lala Hardayal, Sohan Singh Bhakna, Kartar Singh) → a weekly journal.

49-017.r: Amrita Bazar Patrika → founded 1868 by Shishir Kumar Ghosh and Motilal Ghosh (Jessore); Bengali paper turned English overnight in 1878 to escape the Vernacular Press Act.
49-017.t: Don't confuse with 'Bengalee' (Girish Chandra Ghosh, 1862; taken over by S.N. Banerjee).

49-019.r: Tilak → 'Kesari' (Marathi) and 'Mahratta' (English), both started 1881; Kesari's first editor was Gopal Ganesh Agarkar.
49-019.h: Kesari = Marathi, Mahratta = English (the names swap what you expect).

49-020.r: Bangawasi, Kaal and Kesari → all popular papers of the revolutionary period that criticised Congress for its liberal policies.

49-021.r: Sandhya, Yugantar and Kaal → all newspapers that advocated revolutionary terrorism in the freedom struggle.

49-022.r: Young India (Gandhi's weekly preaching non-violence) → not revolutionary; Sandhya, Yugantar and Ghadar were revolutionary papers.

49-023.r: 'Som Prakash' (Bengali weekly, 1858) → started by Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar; first edited by Dwarkanath Vidyabhushan; supported farmers in the Indigo movement.

49-024.r: 'Leader' → mouthpiece of the Liberals; New India → Annie Besant; Young India → Gandhi; Free Press Journal → English daily.

49-025.r: 'Indian Opinion' (Gandhi, South Africa, 1903) → first editor Mansukh Lal Nazar (Secretary of Natal Congress).
49-025.t: Gandhi founded it, but the first editor was Mansukh Lal Nazar.

49-027.r: 'Indian Opinion' → published in Gujarati, Hindi, Tamil and English; not in Urdu.

49-028.r: 'Young India' → began (7 May 1919, Bombay) as a Home Rule League paper (Jamnadas Dwarkadas, Shankar Lal Banker); Gandhi editor from 8 October 1919, weekly from Ahmedabad.

49-029.r: 'Young India' → English weekly nationalist journal, edited by Mahatma Gandhi during 1919–1931.
49-029.c: No answer printed: BPSC deleted the question for writing 'The Young India'.

49-030.r: 'Udant Martand' → first Hindi newspaper, 30 May 1826, from Calcutta (Kolkata); by Pt. Jugal Kishore Shukla, every Tuesday.

49-031.r: 'Hindoo Patriot' (1853) → first English newspaper published by Indians; first editor Girish Chandra Ghosh (1853-55).
49-031.t: Don't pick 'The Hindu' or 'Young India'; Hindoo Patriot was first.

49-032.r: Harish Chandra Mukherjee (editor of Hindoo Patriot from 1855) → strongly supported the Indigo Movement, helping exploited farmers of Bengal.

49-033.r: Aurobindo (Arbind) Ghosh → associated with the English paper 'Vande Mataram'.

49-034.r: 'The Indian Nation' → published from Patna, founded 1931 by Darbhanga King Kameshwar Singh.

49-035.r: K. Ramakrishna Pillai (born 1878, Neyyattinkara, Travancore) → editor of 'Swadeshabhimani'.
49-035.c: Question wrongly names the paper 'Swadesh Vahini'; the book says it is 'Swadeshabhimani'.

49-036.r: English newspaper 'The Independent' → Motilal Nehru; it demanded self-rule for India.

49-037.r: Bharat Mitra → Hindi; Rastra Mata → Marathi; Prajamitra → Gujarati; Nayak → Bengali.

49-038.r: Dainik Aaj → Shiv Prasad Gupta; The Leader → Madan Mohan Malviya; National Herald → Jawaharlal Nehru; The Pioneer → George Allen.

49-039.r: Vijay Singh Pathik → made Bijoliya peasant movement (Mewar; begun 1913 by Sadhu Sitaram Das) known via 'Pratap' of Kanpur (Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi).

49-040.r: Gandhiji → started weeklies 'Harijan' (English), 'Harijan Bandhu' (Gujarati) and 'Harijan Sevak' (Hindi).

49-041.r: Gandhi was not linked with 'Indian Mirror' (Manmohan Ghosh, Debendranath Tagore); he edited Young India, Harijan and Indian Opinion.

49-042.r: 'Harijan' weekly (Gandhi) → first issue on 11 February 1933 from Poona (Pune).

49-043.r: B.R. Ambedkar → Marathi fortnightly 'Bahishkrit Bharat' (1927); earlier founded Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha, Bombay (20 July 1924) for the untouchables.

49-046.r: Abul Kalam Azad → Urdu weekly 'Al-Hilal' (1912; banned in 1914).

49-048.r: Lala Lajpat Rai → Urdu daily 'Vande Matram' (Bande Matram) and English weekly 'The People' from Lahore (1920); earlier 'Young India' in the USA (1916).

49-049.r: Hindu → G. Subramaniya Iyer; Sudharak → Gopal Krishna Gokhale; Voice of India → Dadabhai Naoroji; Bengalee → Surendra Nath Banerjee.

49-050.r: Free Hindustan → Taraknath Das; Indian Opinion → Mahatma Gandhi; Voice of India → Dadabhai Naoroji; Bengalee → Surendranath Banerjee.

49-051.r: Kaal → Shivrama Mahadev Paranjape; Bengalee → Surendra Nath Banerjee; Sudharak → Gokhale; Somaprakash → Dwarkanath Vidyabhushan.

49-052.r: Bombay Chronicle → Feroz Shah Mehta; Commonweal → Annie Besant; Leader → Madan Mohan Malviya; Searchlight → Sachidanand Sinha.

49-053.r: Leader → Madan Mohan Malviya; Bombay Chronicle → Firozshah Mehta; Independent → Motilal Nehru; Justice → T.M. Nair.

49-054.r: Abul Kalam Azad → Al-Hilal; Feroz Shah Mehta → Bombay Chronicle; Annie Besant → New India; Mahatma Gandhi → Young India.

49-055.r: Wrong pair: Tahzeeb-ul-Akhlaq is Sir Syed Ahmed Khan's Urdu journal (1870), not Jinnah's. Correct: Al-Hilal–Azad; New India–Besant; Samvad Kaumudi–Ram Mohan Roy.

49-056.r: Wrong pair: The Pioneer was started by George Allen (Allahabad, 1865), not Gandhi. Gandhi → Indian Opinion, Harijan, Young India, Navjeevan.

49-057.r: 'Yugantar' → Bhupendra Nath Dutt and Barindra Kumar Ghosh, not Gandhi; Gandhi → Indian Opinion, Young India, Nav Jeevan.

49-058.r: 'Qaumi Awaz' → started by Jawaharlal Nehru and Rafi Ahmed Kidwai in 1945 from Lucknow (not Abul Kalam Azad).
49-058.t: Don't pair Qaumi Awaz with Abul Kalam Azad; it was Nehru's.

49-060.r: Commonweal → Annie Besant (correct pair). Also: Mook Nayak → B.R. Ambedkar; Young India → Gandhi; Kesari → Tilak.

49-061.r: Samachar Darpan → J.C. Marshman; Mirat-ul-Akhbar → Raja Ram Mohan Roy; Kesari → B.G. Tilak; Young India → Mahatma Gandhi.

49-062.r: Wrong pair: 'Independent' was Motilal Nehru's, not B.R. Ambedkar's. Correct: Rast Goftar–Dadabhai Naoroji; Kesari–Tilak; New India–Annie Besant.

49-063.r: Places of publication: Swadesh → Gorakhpur; Bharat Bandhu → Hathras; Satyawadi → Agra; Shakti → Almora.

49-064.r: Editors: The Hindu → G. Subramania Iyer; Kesari → Tilak; Bengalee → S.N. Banerjee; Hindustani → Ganga Prasad Verma; Sudharak → Gokhale.

49-065.r: Bal Gangadhar Tilak → Kesari and Mahratta (correct pair); Annie Besant → New India; Mahatma Gandhi → Young India.
49-065.t: Don't swap New India (Besant) with Young India (Gandhi).

49-066.r: Annie Besant → published 'The Commonweal' and 'New India'.
49-066.h: Besant's two: C-N = Commonweal, New India.

49-067.r: 'The Commonweal' → English newspaper from Madras, edited by Annie Besant.

49-068.r: Bipin Chandra Pal → New India; Aurobindo Ghosh → Vande Mataram; Brahma Bandhab Upadhyay → Sandhya; Mohammad Ali → Comrade.

49-069.r: 'Vande Mataram' (English, 1906) → founded by Bipin Chandra Pal, then edited by Aurobindo; Paris edition (10 September 1909) edited by Hardayal, published by Bhikaji Cama.
49-069.c: No answer printed; of the options only Bhikaji Cama fits (publisher of the Paris edition).

49-070.r: 'The Times of India' → not a nationalist paper; The Hindu, Bengalee and The Mahratta → nationalist papers.

49-071.r: 'Dash Roja' periodical → started by Abdul Gaffar Khan during the National Movement.

49-072.r: S.A. Dange → The Socialist; Muzaffar Ahmad → Navyug; Ghulam Husain → Inqilab; M. Singarvelu → Labour Kisan Gazette.

49-073.r: 'The Indian Mirror' (January 1886) → called the Indian National Congress 'the nucleus of a future Parliament of our country'.
